messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
# Clinical Vignette: Robert K.

Robert was sixty-six when he first walked into the office, moving with the careful precision of a man who had spent decades learning not to take up space. At fifty-eight, when his elderly mother had fallen and broken her hip, he had brought her to live with him and his wife, Margaret. Within weeks of her arrival, the old terrors had surfaced with a clarity that shocked him—not the vague anxiety of middle age, but the specific, embodied panic of a child pinned against cold tile.

His mother's hands had been cold, always cold. She would reach out to steady herself on his shoulder, and the shock of that chill against his skin would send him into a state of raw alarm that his conscious mind could not quite justify. When her fingers touched the back of his neck one morning as he poured her coffee, his heart had begun to race so violently he thought he might collapse. The sensation—that particular temperature, that invasive touch—pulled him backward across fifty years to a bathroom in a house he had tried to forget. His father's hands, gripping him under cold running water as punishment for some small infraction, holding him there while his lungs burned and his small body convulsed with shock. The cold had been the instrument and the message: you are not safe, you are not in control, your body is not your own.

The racing of his own heart became its own trigger. Each time it quickened—whether from the coffee he drank too fast or the anxiety that had begun to colonize his mornings—Robert felt the ground shift beneath him. The physical sensation itself was a warning, proof that danger was imminent. And when his mother had reached for him again, or when Margaret had touched his arm in concern, his body had reacted before thought could intervene. He would flinch, sometimes cry out, his nervous system convinced that harm was coming. The intrusive memories came without warning too—a flash of his father's face, the cold, the helplessness—arriving suddenly while Robert was at his desk at work, leaving him shaking and unable to focus on code that had once been his refuge.

What had begun as isolated moments of discomfort had calcified into a set of certainties that now governed his days. Robert had come to believe that he had to be constantly vigilant, that the world contained threats he could not predict or control, that people—even those who loved him—could not be trusted with his vulnerability. The more he thought about these dangers, the more he noticed them everywhere. He began to scan rooms for potential weapons, for objects that could be used to harm him. He saw the kitchen knife differently now. He saw the belt Margaret hung by the door. These were not threats in any rational sense, but his mind had learned to read danger in the ordinary architecture of domestic life. And these vigilant observations only deepened his conviction that he was right to be afraid, that his constant carefulness was justified, necessary, the only thing keeping him safe.

To manage the panic, Robert had withdrawn. He stopped looking at his own body in the shower, unable to bear the sight of his skin without feeling exposed and vulnerable. He began declining invitations from the colleagues he had socialized with for years—the monthly dinners, the weekend hiking trips—telling himself that being around people meant being at risk, meant having to endure the possibility of unexpected touch. Most painfully, he had pulled away from Margaret's affection. She had tried to understand, had asked what was wrong, but he could not explain that her hand on his back felt like a threat, that her attempt to comfort him felt like an invasion. The avoidance had seemed protective at first, a way to maintain control. But as weeks turned into months, the isolation had only intensified his belief that he was fundamentally damaged, permanently set apart from others, an outsider in his own marriage and his own life.

The cycle had tightened relentlessly. His avoidance of touch meant he remained hypervigilant to the possibility of it, scanning for the moment when someone might breach his boundary. His withdrawal from his body meant he was more attuned to its signals—every flutter of his heart felt dangerous, every unexpected sensation a harbinger. And each time he managed to avoid contact, each time he successfully isolated himself, the conviction that people could not be trusted, that he needed constant vigilance, grew stronger. Margaret had finally insisted he see someone, her own distress evident. Robert had agreed, though he remained uncertain whether anyone could help him understand why, after so many decades, the cold still had such power, and why the people closest to him now felt like the greatest threat of all.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette depicts triggers (his mother's cold hands, racing heart, touch) and negative appraisals (beliefs about constant vigilance, untrustworthiness, danger everywhere) but does not establish a causal pathway showing that triggers directly drive or lead to the formation or intensification of these appraisals—only that both exist and interact through other mechanisms.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
His father's hands, gripping him under cold running water as punishment for some small infraction, holding him there while his lungs burned and his small body convulsed with shock. The cold had been the instrument and the message: you are not safe, you are not in control, your body is not your own.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Now, each time his mother's cold fingers found his shoulder or his own heart began to race unbidden, the old message returned with it: danger was real, it was close, and he could never fully protect himself from it. These moments of panic did not feel like echoes of the past—they felt like proof that the world remained as unsafe as it had always been.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
When her fingers touched the back of his neck one morning as he poured her coffee, his heart had begun to race so violently he thought he might collapse. The sensation—that particular temperature, that invasive touch—pulled him backward across fifty years to a bathroom in a house he had tried to forget.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
And in that pulling backward, something crystallized: if these innocent gestures could trigger such terror, then people themselves—even Margaret, even his mother—must be sources of threat he could not predict or control. The logic felt airtight, inevitable.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Each time it quickened—whether from the coffee he drank too fast or the anxiety that had begun to colonize his mornings—Robert felt the ground shift beneath him. The physical sensation itself was a warning, proof that danger was imminent.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Every flutter of his pulse told him that he was right to be afraid, that his hypervigilance was not paranoia but clarity, the only honest way to read a world that had shown him its teeth long ago.
<<<END>>>
